transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

Hi… yeah, I came in because it’s getting hard to explain myself clearly, I think. I’m an artist, so I’m used to talking in a kind of layered way about materials and texture and meaning, but lately it’s like my thoughts don’t stay in one lane. I’ll be writing an artist statement and I start with the surface of a piece, like the texture or color, and then suddenly I’m talking about the budget for the project, and then it turns into these… hidden or secret meanings I think are connected, but when someone reads it back they say it doesn’t make sense.

It’s happening in client notes too, not just art writing, and even in meetings. I’ll be trying to answer a straightforward question and I can feel myself jumping around—textures, money, symbols, what something “really” means underneath—and people keep looking confused or telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to say. It’s embarrassing, because in my head it feels connected, but when it comes out, apparently it’s not coming across that way.

When you talk about these hidden or secret meanings that you feel are connected, do you believe something specific is being communicated or hidden in the materials—like a message only you can understand?

Yeah… I mean, I know how it sounds, but yes, sometimes it feels very specific. Like it’s not just that I’m interpreting something creatively or making associations for an artwork. I’ll see a stain on a studio floor, or the way two pieces of fabric meet at a seam, or even a phrase in an email from a gallery, and it feels like it’s meant for me in particular.

Not always in a dramatic way, but like… instructions, almost. Or warnings. Like if a seam is pulling apart in a certain place, I’ll think it means I’m supposed to change the direction of the piece, or that if I keep going the way I’m going something will go wrong with the work. And with emails, if someone uses a certain phrase—something ordinary, probably—I can get stuck on it and feel like they’re hinting at something underneath, like they’re telling me what I should do without saying it directly.

The hard part is that even when someone explains it in a normal way—like, “That’s just a coffee stain,” or “That’s just how the email was worded”—I can understand their explanation intellectually, but it doesn’t really loosen the feeling. It still feels aimed at me. Like there’s a message there and I’m supposed to catch it.
Have there been times when you felt so certain about one of these hidden messages that you changed your behavior or made decisions based on it, even if others didn’t see the connection?

Yes. Yeah, that has happened. Not in a way where I’m like, announcing it to everyone, but I’ll quietly change what I’m doing because the feeling is so strong.

Like with stains in the studio—there was one time I kept noticing this mark on the floor near where I was working, and it was probably just paint or coffee or something, but it looked positioned in this really specific way. I couldn’t stop feeling like it was pointing to a decision I was supposed to make with the piece, like a warning that the direction I was going in was wrong. So I changed the composition around it. I spent hours reworking something because it felt like the stain was telling me not to ignore it.

And seams do that too. If fabric pulls or folds in a certain place, I can get convinced it means something about the work, like the piece is resisting me or showing me where the problem is. Sometimes that’s probably just normal art-making intuition, but this feels different. It feels addressed to me, almost like instructions.

Gallery emails are harder because those involve other people. If someone uses a phrase that feels loaded, I’ll read it over and over and adjust how I respond, or delay sending something, or change what I planned to submit because I feel like they’re warning me without directly saying it. Even if someone else reads the email and says, “No, that’s just a normal sentence,” I can understand that logically, but the certainty doesn’t really go away. I still feel like I’m supposed to act on it.

Have you ever experienced thoughts or feelings that other people don’t seem to share, like things in the world around you have special meaning or are communicating with you in a way that you know might not make sense to others—even though it feels very real to you?

Yes… that’s pretty much exactly what I mean. I get this feeling that certain things around me are not just random, even if I know other people would say they are. Like stains on the floor, or the way a seam comes together or pulls apart, or a phrase in a gallery email—something ordinary like that can feel like it’s meant specifically for me.

It can feel like an instruction or a warning about the work, like I’m supposed to notice it and respond. And I can tell myself, okay, maybe this is just a stain, or maybe the email is just written in a normal professional way, but the feeling doesn’t really let go. It still feels like there’s something underneath it, like I’m being told something indirectly.

I know it probably sounds strange when I say it out loud, and I don’t always talk about it because I can tell people don’t see what I’m seeing. But in the moment it feels very real and very directed at me, and it’s hard to ignore.
Even though you know others might not share your interpretation of these signs, do you still feel certain they are real messages meant for you, regardless of what others say?

Yes… I do. I mean, I can say “maybe I’m wrong” because I know that’s what other people would say, and part of me can understand that. But when it’s happening, it doesn’t feel like an interpretation. It feels like the thing is there for me to notice.

Like a stain might be just a stain to someone else, but if it’s in a certain place or has a certain shape, I can get completely convinced it’s pointing me toward something I’m supposed to change in the work. Or if a seam pulls in a strange way, it feels like a warning, like the piece is telling me something is wrong. And with gallery emails, even one phrase can feel loaded, like they’re indirectly telling me what to do or what not to do.

People can explain it in a normal way, and I can hear them. I’m not trying to be difficult. But the feeling doesn’t really go away just because someone says, “No, that’s ordinary.” It still feels meant for me, and it’s very hard to let go of.
Have you ever had experiences where you felt certain something was real or true, even though you know most people would say it’s impossible or doesn’t make sense at all?

Yes… although I don’t usually think of it as “impossible” in the moment. That’s the hard part. If I’m calm and talking to you right now, I can hear how it sounds, like stains or seams or email wording shouldn’t be able to mean anything beyond what they are. I know most people would say, “That’s just a mark on the floor,” or “That’s just how the fabric folded,” or “That gallery email is just a normal professional email.”

But when it happens, it feels true in a way that’s really difficult to argue with. Like I’ll see a stain near where I’m working, and it’s not just that I notice it visually—it feels placed, almost like it’s there to get my attention. Or a seam will pull in this particular way, and I’ll feel like it’s warning me that something about the work is wrong. With emails, a phrase can feel like it has a second meaning, like they’re telling me something indirectly without actually saying it.

And even if someone explains it in a totally ordinary way, I can understand the explanation, but I don’t fully believe it. Or I believe it intellectually, maybe, but emotionally it still feels like the message is real and meant for me. I’ll keep turning it over in my head, and it can be very hard to let go of.

Have there been times when you felt certain that something was happening to you—like being watched, followed, or communicated with—based on subtle signs that others might not notice, even though you know others might not agree that it's happening?

Yes… I think so, though for me it’s less like being followed in a literal way and more like being communicated with through things that other people would probably pass right over. It’s usually very subtle, which is part of why it’s hard to explain without sounding… I don’t know, like I’m making connections that aren’t there.

For example, I’ll notice a stain on the floor near where I’m working, and if it has a certain shape or it’s in a certain spot, I can get really convinced it’s not accidental. It feels like it’s pointing to something I need to fix or change in the work. Or with seams—if a seam pulls apart or gathers in a certain way, it can feel like a warning, like the piece is telling me something is wrong. And gallery emails are a big one. A phrase that’s probably completely normal can feel loaded, like there’s a message underneath it that’s meant specifically for me.

I know other people might say, “That’s just a stain,” or “That’s just fabric behaving normally,” or “That’s just a professional email,” and I can understand that explanation on some level. But when I’m in it, I feel certain. Not just interested or curious—certain. And even after someone gives me a normal explanation, it can still sit in my mind for a long time, like I’m supposed to keep paying attention to it. It’s very hard to let go of.

Have you ever felt that thoughts were being placed in your mind that weren’t your own, or that events, actions, or objects around you were directly related to you in a personal way that others couldn’t see?

I don’t really feel like thoughts are being placed in my mind, not in that exact way. It doesn’t feel like someone is inserting thoughts, if that makes sense. The thoughts feel like mine, but they get… attached to things around me in a way that feels very personal and hard to shake.

Like I’ve said, it happens with stains or seams or even wording in gallery emails. A stain won’t just look like a stain to me sometimes—it’ll feel like it’s there for me, like it’s marking something I’m supposed to notice. Or if a seam is pulling strangely, I can become convinced it’s a warning about the piece, like I need to change something before I continue. And with emails, a phrase can feel like it has this hidden instruction in it, even if I know the person probably just wrote it normally.

I can usually understand afterward that other people wouldn’t see it that way. If someone says, “No, that’s just a normal email,” or “That’s just how the fabric is behaving,” I can follow their reasoning. But it doesn’t completely undo the feeling. It still feels directed at me, like there’s something I’m supposed to take from it, and then I keep thinking about it over and over. It’s not easy for me to just dismiss it.

Have you ever felt that things happening around you—like events, people’s actions, or even objects—were directly and personally related to you in a way that others didn’t seem to notice or understand?

Yes, that’s exactly more how it feels. Not usually like some big dramatic thing, but like small things around me are… not random, I guess. Like they’re connected to me and my work in a way other people don’t pick up on.

A stain on the floor, for example, can start to feel like it’s there for a reason, like it’s pointing something out to me. Or if I’m working with fabric or a piece and a seam is pulling in a certain way, I can get really convinced it’s a warning or instruction—like I’m supposed to stop, change something, fix something, rethink the whole piece. And with gallery emails, it can be a phrase that I’m sure has another layer to it, like they’re telling me something indirectly about what I should do or what I’ve done wrong, even if the words themselves are totally normal.

I do know, sitting here, that someone else would probably say, “No, that’s just a stain,” or “That’s just how seams behave,” or “That’s just professional wording.” And sometimes someone has explained it to me that way, and I can understand it logically. But it doesn’t always loosen the feeling. It can stay with me, like I missed the real message if I ignore it. I’ll keep turning it over and over, trying to figure out what it means, and it’s very hard to just drop it.

Have you ever felt that things happening around you—like events, people’s actions, or even objects—were directly and personally related to you in ways that weren’t connected to your art or your work, in everyday situations that others didn’t seem to notice or understand?

I’m trying to think of examples that aren’t tied to my work, and honestly… it’s harder for me to separate them, because so much of where this happens is around making things or dealing with galleries.

Like, the clearest ones are still the stains, seams, and emails. A stain on the floor might seem everyday, but when it happens near where I’m working, I can get very convinced it’s meant for me somehow, like it’s pointing out something I need to notice. Or a seam doing something strange can feel like an instruction or warning about the piece. And with gallery emails, even a normal phrase can feel like it has this hidden meaning directed at me personally.

Outside of that context, I don’t know if I’d say it happens as clearly. I’m not sure I have a good example of, like, a random person’s action on the street or some unrelated event feeling personally about me. It’s more that ordinary things become charged when they’re near the work or somehow connected to it. And even if someone gives me a reasonable explanation—like, “that’s just a stain,” or “that’s normal wording”—I can understand that, but the feeling doesn’t always go away. It still feels like I’m supposed to pay attention to it.

Have you ever felt that things people said or did in everyday life—like things you heard on the street, saw online, or experienced in public—were directed at you personally, even if they weren’t related to your art or galleries?

Not really in a clear way outside of the art or gallery context. I mean, I can be sensitive to things people say in general, but when you say, like, something I hear on the street or see online feeling personally directed at me… I don’t have a strong example of that.

For me it’s much more around the work. That’s where things start feeling like they’re meant specifically for me. A stain, a seam, a phrase in an email from a gallery—those can feel like they’re carrying some instruction or warning, like I’m supposed to understand something from them that isn’t obvious on the surface. And I can get really stuck on it.

Even if someone says, “That’s just normal wording,” or “That’s just a mark on the floor,” I can sort of understand what they mean, but I don’t fully feel convinced. It still feels like there’s something there for me, and if I ignore it, I worry I’m missing the message. So everyday public things, not so much—but ordinary things connected to my work, yes, definitely.

Have you ever felt that things people said or did in everyday life—like things you heard on the street, saw online, or experienced in public—were directed at you personally, even if they weren’t related to your art or galleries?

I know you’re asking specifically outside of the art and gallery stuff, and I don’t really have a strong example like overhearing someone on the street and thinking they were talking to me, or seeing some random post online and feeling like it was aimed at me personally.

For me it’s much more… it happens through the work, or around the work. Like certain stains, or the way a seam is sitting or pulling, or even a phrase in a gallery email. Those can feel very specifically meant for me, like they’re not just incidental. They feel like instructions or warnings, like I’m supposed to understand something from them about what I’m making or what I’ve done wrong or what I need to change.

And the hard part is that even if someone gives me a normal explanation—like, “That’s just a stain,” or “That’s just how the fabric is behaving,” or “That’s just professional email language”—I can hear that and understand it, but I don’t always feel convinced. It can still feel like there’s a message there, and if I let it go, I’m ignoring something important. So, in everyday public life, not really in the same way. It’s mostly those work-connected things that get that personal meaning attached to them.
Have you ever believed something strongly that turned out to be completely untrue, and even when people gave you clear evidence, you still couldn’t let go of that belief?

Yes… I think that does happen, though I still hesitate with the word “completely untrue,” because in the moment it doesn’t feel untrue to me. It feels very real and specific.

The main examples are the ones I’ve been talking about—the stains, seams, and phrases in gallery emails. Like if there’s a stain near where I’m working, I can become really convinced it’s there for a reason, like it’s pointing something out about the work or telling me I’ve made a wrong decision. Or if a seam is pulling in a certain way, I might read it almost like an instruction, like I’m supposed to change the piece, or it’s warning me not to send it out yet. And with emails, sometimes a totally ordinary phrase from a gallery can feel loaded, like there’s a message inside it meant only for me.

Other people can explain it very clearly—“that’s just a stain,” or “fabric does that,” or “they’re just using normal professional language”—and I can understand the explanation intellectually. I’m not unable to hear them. But emotionally, or in my gut, I don’t let go of it easily. I keep circling back to it and thinking, no, there’s something there, I’m supposed to notice this, and if I ignore it then I’m missing something important.

So yes, I guess I have believed those things very strongly even when someone else had a much more ordinary explanation. It’s not always dramatic from the outside, but inside it can become very fixed.

Have you ever had a belief that something was happening to you—like someone was trying to communicate with you through everyday things—that you held onto strongly, even when there was no real proof or when others gave you good reasons to think otherwise?

Yes. I mean, that’s probably the clearest way to describe what happens, even though it’s hard for me to call it that in the moment.

It’s usually not like I think a person is secretly sending me messages in some obvious way. It’s more that certain things around my work start feeling… too specific to be accidental. Like a stain on the floor or on fabric, or the way a seam is sitting, or some phrase in an email from a gallery. I can get really convinced that it’s meant for me somehow, like it’s an instruction or a warning about the work—like I’m being told I made the wrong choice, or I need to change something, or I shouldn’t send it out yet.

And people can give me very reasonable explanations. They’ll say, “That’s just a stain,” or “That seam is pulling because of the material,” or “That’s just normal gallery email language.” And I can understand what they’re saying. I’m not completely unable to follow the logic. But it doesn’t really settle it for me. I’ll still feel like, no, there’s something there, and if I ignore it, I’m missing something important.

So yes, I have held onto that kind of belief pretty strongly, even without real proof. It can be very hard to let go of once I’ve attached meaning to it.

Have you ever believed something so strongly that you felt it was undeniably true, even when there was clear evidence or multiple people telling you otherwise, and this belief wasn't just about your work or art but could have involved other areas of your life?

I think… if you’re asking whether it happens outside the work or art context, I don’t really have another clear area of my life that comes to mind. It’s not like I can give you an example from dating, or neighbors, or something on the news where I was absolutely sure it was about me. The strongest, most undeniable-feeling beliefs are still around my work.

But within that, yes, it can feel completely true at the time. Like if there’s a stain in a certain place, or a seam is pulling in a way that feels significant, or a gallery email uses a phrase that suddenly feels pointed, I can get very convinced that it’s meant specifically for me. Not just “oh, that’s interesting,” but like it’s an instruction or a warning—like I’m being told I did something wrong, or I need to change the piece, or I shouldn’t move forward.

And other people can be very clear with me. They can say, “This is just how the fabric is behaving,” or “That’s just a normal phrase,” or show me some ordinary reason for it. I can understand what they’re saying, but it doesn’t always make the belief go away. It still feels like there’s a message in it, and letting it go feels almost irresponsible, like I’m ignoring something I was supposed to notice.

So… not really in other areas, at least not that I can identify. But with the work-related things, yes, I can hold onto it very strongly even when people are telling me there’s a normal explanation.

Have you ever had a strong belief about something happening in your life—like someone trying to communicate with you, give you a message, or something being specifically about you—that wasn’t related to your work or art, and that you held onto even when there was no clear evidence or when others tried to convince you otherwise?

Not really outside of my work, no—or at least I can’t think of a clean example where it wasn’t tied back to the art somehow.

The thing is, my work is so woven into my day that sometimes it’s hard for me to separate “life” from “work.” So if there’s a stain on fabric, or a mark on the floor near where I’m working, or a seam that’s pulling in a certain way, or even a phrase in an email from a gallery, it can feel like it’s specifically meant for me. Like not just random, not just coincidence, but almost like an instruction or a warning. Like I’m supposed to change something, or stop, or not send something out, or notice that I’ve made the wrong decision.

But if you mean something totally separate from that—like someone communicating with me through the TV, or strangers on the street, or something unrelated to the studio—I don’t really have that. The strong beliefs I’m talking about are mostly centered on the work and the things around it.

And even when people explain it in a normal way, like “that’s just how the fabric is sitting” or “that’s a standard phrase in a professional email,” I can hear them, but I don’t always believe it in my body. I’ll keep coming back to it and feeling like, no, there is something there, and if I ignore it I’m missing the message. So… outside of work, not that I can identify, but within that world, yes, I can hold onto it really strongly.

Have you ever believed something was happening to you that you know other people would say is impossible, even beyond the messages you feel in your work—like something completely outside of reality as most people understand it?

I don’t think so—not in the way you mean, like something totally outside reality or impossible in a big, obvious way. I’m not walking around thinking, you know, gravity stopped working or that someone is controlling the weather for me or something like that.

For me it stays more in this specific lane, which I know I keep coming back to, but that’s honestly where it happens. It’s the stains, or the seams, or little things in the studio, or wording in gallery emails. Those can feel like they’re meant for me in a way that other people would probably say is not real, or at least not reasonable. Like they’ll say, “That’s just a mark,” or “That email is just standard wording,” and I can understand that on one level, but I still get stuck on it.

It can feel very much like an instruction or a warning about the work—like I’m supposed to change something, or hold back, or notice that I made the wrong choice. And it’s hard because I don’t always experience it as “I’m making this up.” It feels meaningful, like it has a pressure behind it. Even when someone gives me a completely ordinary explanation, it doesn’t just dissolve.

But beyond that—beyond those messages or meanings around the work—I don’t really have an example of believing something completely impossible was happening to me. It’s more that ordinary things start feeling personally directed and significant, and then I have trouble letting that go.

Have you ever believed something was happening to you that you knew was impossible or not real, even beyond the meanings you sometimes see in your work—like events that could not possibly happen in the real world?

I don’t think I have examples of, like, impossible events exactly. I know you’re asking if I believed something that couldn’t happen in the real world, and… no, not really in that big way.

What does happen is more like ordinary things start feeling not ordinary. Like a stain on fabric will be in a particular place, or a seam will pull a certain way, or an email from a gallery will have one phrase that catches me, and I’ll feel very convinced that it’s meant for me. Not just “that’s interesting,” but like it’s an instruction or a warning about the work. Like I’m supposed to change the piece, or stop sending it out, or take it as a sign that I did something wrong.

And I can know, at least intellectually, that someone else would say, “That’s just a stain,” or “That’s just how the fabric folded,” or “That’s normal gallery wording.” Sometimes someone will actually show me that, and I can follow what they’re saying. But it doesn’t always loosen the feeling. It still feels directed at me, like there’s something I’m supposed to understand from it, and if I ignore it I’m being careless.

So no, I don’t think I’ve believed in events that literally couldn’t happen. It’s more that these real, normal things get this meaning attached to them, and once that happens it’s really hard for me to let it go.

Have you ever had a belief that something was happening in your life—like someone was trying to send you a message, follow you, or influence you in some way—that wasn’t related to your art or work, and that you held onto even when there was no clear evidence it was true?

I know I’ve kind of answered this in a few different ways already, but… if you mean totally outside the art, then I don’t really have a strong example of that.

It’s not usually like I think someone is following me, or influencing me from somewhere, or sending me messages through completely unrelated things. It’s more that my work creates this whole environment where those feelings happen. Like I’ll see a stain on fabric, or the way a seam is pulling, or even a phrase in a gallery email, and it can feel very specifically directed at me. Not just “oh, that’s odd,” but like it means something I’m supposed to act on.

It can feel like an instruction, almost. Or a warning. Like I shouldn’t send the piece, or I need to change something, or I made the wrong decision and the mark is pointing it out. And then if someone says, “No, that’s just how the fabric folded,” or “That’s just normal wording, they send that to everyone,” I can understand what they’re saying, but it doesn’t always actually convince me. I’ll keep feeling like there’s something I’m missing if I dismiss it.

So… outside of the work, no, not really that I can identify. But around the work, yes, I can get very fixed on those meanings, even when there isn’t clear evidence and even when someone gives me a much more ordinary explanation.

Have you ever had a belief about something happening to you that you knew made no sense at all, even to you at the time—like something that couldn’t possibly be true in the real world, even beyond the meanings you sometimes see in your work?

I don’t know that I’ve had something where, even in the moment, I thought, “This makes no sense at all and couldn’t possibly be true,” and still believed it in that kind of obvious impossible way. I don’t usually have it like… some event that breaks reality, if that makes sense.

It’s more subtle, but it still gets really strong. Like with the stains or seams in my work, or even a certain phrase in a gallery email, I can become really convinced that it’s not accidental. It feels meant for me specifically, like it’s telling me something—almost like an instruction or a warning about the piece. And I know that probably sounds like I’m just making meaning out of normal things, and sometimes I can even say that to myself, but it doesn’t feel that simple when it’s happening.

Someone can point out, “That’s just where the fabric folded,” or “That’s just standard wording,” and I can understand the explanation. I’m not unable to hear it. But emotionally, or somewhere deeper, I still feel like there’s a message there and I’m being careless if I ignore it. So it’s not that I think something physically impossible happened. It’s more that ordinary things start feeling directed at me, and then I get stuck on that meaning even when the reasonable explanation is right in front of me.

inference_history.note: The patient's description of experiencing hidden or secret meanings in everyday stimuli (e.g., stains, seams, phrases in emails), along with disorganized thought patterns (jumping between topics that feel internally connected but not logically so), supports the presence of thought disorder and ideas of reference. These features are commonly seen in schizophrenia spectrum disorders. This rules out bipolar I disorder (F31.0, F31.1, F31.2) and mania (F30.1, F30.2) as primary explanations, as the symptom profile is more consistent with a psychotic disorder rather than a mood episode.

The patient's descriptions of experiencing hidden or symbolic meanings in ordinary events, along with the impact of these experiences on their behavior and decision-making, support the presence of delusional-like ideas or overvalued ideas. This reduces the likelihood of F20.8 (Other schizophrenia) as a primary diagnosis, which typically requires more prominent and diverse psychotic symptoms not yet captured here. The remaining candidates all include features of delusions, thought disorder, and/or scholastic or affective components consistent with the patient's presentation.

The thing is, my work is so woven into my day that sometimes it’s hard for me to separate “life” from “work.” So if there’s a stain on fabric, or a mark on the floor near where I’m working, or a seam that’s pulling in a certain way, or even a phrase in an email from a gallery, it can feel like it’s specifically meant for me. Like not just random, not just coincidence, but almost like an instruction or a warning. Like I’m supposed to change something, or stop, or not send something out, or notice that I’ve made the wrong decision.

But if you mean something totally separate from that—like someone communicating with me through the TV, or strangers on the street, or something unrelated to the studio—I don’t really have that. The strong beliefs I’m talking about are mostly centered on the work and the things around it.

And even when people explain it in a normal way, like “that’s just how the fabric is sitting” or “that’s a standard phrase in a professional email,” I can hear them, but I don’t always believe it in my body. I’ll keep coming back to it and feeling like, no, there is something there, and if I ignore it I’m missing the message. So… outside of work, not that I can identify, but within that world, yes, I can hold onto it really strongly.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so—not in the way you mean, like something totally outside reality or impossible in a big, obvious way. I’m not walking around thinking, you know, gravity stopped working or that someone is controlling the weather for me or something like that.

For me it stays more in this specific lane, which I know I keep coming back to, but that’s honestly where it happens. It’s the stains, or the seams, or little things in the studio, or wording in gallery emails. Those can feel like they’re meant for me in a way that other people would probably say is not real, or at least not reasonable. Like they’ll say, “That’s just a mark,” or “That email is just standard wording,” and I can understand that on one level, but I still get stuck on it.

It can feel very much like an instruction or a warning about the work—like I’m supposed to change something, or hold back, or notice that I made the wrong choice. And it’s hard because I don’t always experience it as “I’m making this up.” It feels meaningful, like it has a pressure behind it. Even when someone gives me a completely ordinary explanation, it doesn’t just dissolve.

But beyond that—beyond those messages or meanings around the work—I don’t really have an example of believing something completely impossible was happening to me. It’s more that ordinary things start feeling personally directed and significant, and then I have trouble letting that go.

patient.answer:
I don’t think I have examples of, like, impossible events exactly. I know you’re asking if I believed something that couldn’t happen in the real world, and… no, not really in that big way.

What does happen is more like ordinary things start feeling not ordinary. Like a stain on fabric will be in a particular place, or a seam will pull a certain way, or an email from a gallery will have one phrase that catches me, and I’ll feel very convinced that it’s meant for me. Not just “that’s interesting,” but like it’s an instruction or a warning about the work. Like I’m supposed to change the piece, or stop sending it out, or take it as a sign that I did something wrong.

And I can know, at least intellectually, that someone else would say, “That’s just a stain,” or “That’s just how the fabric folded,” or “That’s normal gallery wording.” Sometimes someone will actually show me that, and I can follow what they’re saying. But it doesn’t always loosen the feeling. It still feels directed at me, like there’s something I’m supposed to understand from it, and if I ignore it I’m being careless.

So no, I don’t think I’ve believed in events that literally couldn’t happen. It’s more that these real, normal things get this meaning attached to them, and once that happens it’s really hard for me to let it go.

doctor.question: Have you ever had a belief that something was happening in your life—like someone was trying to send you a message, follow you, or influence you in some way—that wasn’t related to your art or work, and that you held onto even when there was no clear evidence it was true?

patient.answer:
I know I’ve kind of answered this in a few different ways already, but… if you mean totally outside the art, then I don’t really have a strong example of that.

It’s not usually like I think someone is following me, or influencing me from somewhere, or sending me messages through completely unrelated things. It’s more that my work creates this whole environment where those feelings happen. Like I’ll see a stain on fabric, or the way a seam is pulling, or even a phrase in a gallery email, and it can feel very specifically directed at me. Not just “oh, that’s odd,” but like it means something I’m supposed to act on.

It can feel like an instruction, almost. Or a warning. Like I shouldn’t send the piece, or I need to change something, or I made the wrong decision and the mark is pointing it out. And then if someone says, “No, that’s just how the fabric folded,” or “That’s just normal wording, they send that to everyone,” I can understand what they’re saying, but it doesn’t always actually convince me. I’ll keep feeling like there’s something I’m missing if I dismiss it.

So… outside of the work, no, not really that I can identify. But around the work, yes, I can get very fixed on those meanings, even when there isn’t clear evidence and even when someone gives me a much more ordinary explanation.

doctor.question: Have you ever had a belief about something happening to you that you knew made no sense at all, even to you at the time—like something that couldn’t possibly be true in the real world, even beyond the meanings you sometimes see in your work?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I get convinced that certain stains, seams, or phrases in gallery emails are meant specifically for me, like instructions or warnings about my work, and it is very hard to let go of that even when someone shows me a more ordinary explanation.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fixed false or impossible beliefs and whether the patient held them despite recognizing they made no sense, which directly relates to delusions.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’ve had something where, even in the moment, I thought, “This makes no sense at all and couldn’t possibly be true,” and still believed it in that kind of obvious impossible way. I don’t usually have it like… some event that breaks reality, if that makes sense.

It’s more subtle, but it still gets really strong. Like with the stains or seams in my work, or even a certain phrase in a gallery email, I can become really convinced that it’s not accidental. It feels meant for me specifically, like it’s telling me something—almost like an instruction or a warning about the piece. And I know that probably sounds like I’m just making meaning out of normal things, and sometimes I can even say that to myself, but it doesn’t feel that simple when it’s happening.

Someone can point out, “That’s just where the fabric folded,” or “That’s just standard wording,” and I can understand the explanation. I’m not unable to hear it. But emotionally, or somewhere deeper, I still feel like there’s a message there and I’m being careless if I ignore it. So it’s not that I think something physically impossible happened. It’s more that ordinary things start feeling directed at me, and then I get stuck on that meaning even when the reasonable explanation is right in front of me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a persistent and fixed belief that ordinary events and objects in their environment (e.g., stains, seams, email phrases) carry special, personally directed meanings. These beliefs are non-bizarre in nature, as they involve real-world items interpreted with idiosyncratic significance, and are consistent with delusions of reference. There is no evidence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech beyond tangentiality related to the delusional content, or grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior. The delusional system appears to be well-systematized around the theme of personal communication through environmental cues, primarily in the context of their artistic work, with preserved functioning in other domains. Duration is chronic, with no significant deterioration of functioning, which supports a diagnosis of paranoid-type schizophrenia (F20.0) over other schizophrenia subtypes or delusional disorder.
